newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Violence flares as Indonesia campaign nears end.
newsitem.headline: Violence flares as Indonesia campaign nears end.

text.p: Clashes broke out overnight in the Indonesian capital Jakarta between supporters of rival parties contesting the May 29 elections, witnesses said on Thursday.

They said loyalists of the Moslem-based United Development Party (PPP) and the ruling Golkar party threw stones at each other in the central Matraman district late on Wednesday. Police broke up the fighting.
There were no reports of serious injuries or arrests.
Violence has been intensifying as the four-week campaign draws to a close on Friday.
Police and the military said strict security would be in force in Jakarta on Friday, when the PPP is scheduled to make its last appeals to the electorate on the main island of Java.
There were no immediate reports of violence on Thursday, with the Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI) marking its last day of campaigning on Java, police said.
"It's quiet today, but we never know what will happen in the next few hours. What I can say now is that we are beefing up security," one policeman told Reuters by telephone.

The official Antara news agency quoted Jakarta military commander Major-General Sutiyoso as saying about 20,000 men from the army, navy, air force and police were on duty in the capital and had strict orders to clamp down on violence.

"The security officers will act upon and handle directly any signs of disturbances, and the people are called upon to remain calm and not to be easily incited into violent acts," Sutiyoso was quoted as saying.

Analysts have described the violence in this year's campaign as unprecedented. Most of it has been limited to Java, home to some 60 percent of the country's 200 million population, and has involved PPP supporters and Golkar rivals and the police.
Golkar, the PPP and the PDI are the only parties legally permitted to contest the elections. Under pre-election arrangements, each party campaigns in a separate part of the country each day.

Golkar, in power for the last 30 years, is seeking to boost its support to more than 70 percent of the vote from 68 percent in the last elections in 1992. Analysts have said it is likely to win easily, but they are divided on whether the party will increase its share of the vote.
Authorities have scheduled a five-day cooling off period between the end of the campaign and polling day.
